This vignette demonstrates two ways to use covariates in `compphysiol`:

- nonlinear regression, where covariates explain differences between
  individuals and no unexplained individual variability is estimated;
- nonlinear mixed-effects modelling, where covariate effects and unexplained
  individual variability are estimated together.

The examples use body weight as a continuous covariate and sex as a categorical
covariate. The same dynamic model is used in both analyses.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(compphysiol)
library(units)
library(ggplot2)

has_nlmixr2 <- requireNamespace("nlmixr2est", quietly = TRUE)
```

## Where covariates belong

Covariate modelling uses existing model components rather than a separate
covariate object:

- an experiment's `parameters` contain the observed covariate values for one
  individual;
- model `equations` define how covariates affect structural parameters;
- `parameter_specs` identify the shared coefficients to estimate;
- a `statistical_model` adds unexplained individual variability and observation
  error when required.

Experiment parameters are known values. They cannot simultaneously be shared
estimated parameters. In particular, the individual body weights and sex
indicators below are inputs, whereas the body-weight exponent and sex effect
are estimated coefficients.

## Dynamic and covariate model

Consider a one-compartment intravenous model. Clearance depends on body weight
and sex, whereas volume is shared across individuals:

\[
CL_i = CL_{ref}
       \left(\frac{BW_i}{BW_{ref}}\right)^{\theta_{BW}}
       \exp(\beta_{female} female_i).
\]

Here, `female` is zero for the reference category and one for the female
category. Consequently, `exp(beta_female)` is the female-to-reference clearance
ratio at the same body weight.

```{r}
#| label: dynamic-model
model <- compartment_model() |>
    add_compartment(name = "Central", volume = "V") |>
    add_molecule(
        name = "drug",
        cmt = "Central",
        initial = 0 [mg],
        type = "amount"
    ) |>
    add_transport(
        from = "Central",
        to = NULL,
        molec = "drug",
        rate = "CL * c[drug, Central]"
    ) |>
    add_equation(
        CL = CLref * (BW / BWref)^theta_BW *
            exp(beta_female * female)
    ) |>
    add_observable(C = c[drug, Central]) |>
    add_parameter(BWref = 70 [kg])

model
```

`BWref` fixes the interpretation of `CLref`: it is clearance for an individual
in the reference sex category at 70 kg. It is usually preferable to choose and
fix this reference value rather than estimate it together with `CLref`.

## From tabular data to experiments

The example data are stored as an ordinary CSV file installed with the package.
It has one row per observation and contains identifiers, observation times,
concentrations, body weights, and categorical sex labels. CSV files cannot
retain physical units, so units are attached immediately after import.

```{r}
#| label: import-data
data_file <- system.file(
    "extdata", "covariate-pk.csv",
    package = "compphysiol"
)
covariate_data <- read.csv(data_file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

covariate_data <- with_units(within(covariate_data, {
    time <- time [h]
    concentration <- concentration [mg/L]
    bw <- bw [kg]
}))

head(covariate_data)
```

The original categorical labels remain useful for inspection and plotting. The
numerical model receives an explicit contrast encoding instead: `female` is one
for female individuals and zero for the male reference category. Making this
step visible avoids an implicit choice of reference level or contrast
convention.

Each individual becomes one experiment. Covariates that are constant within an
individual are stored as known experiment parameters, while the observation
rows become `observation_data`. The common dose is part of every experiment.

```{r}
#| label: construct-experiments
subject_rows <- split(covariate_data, covariate_data$id)

study_list <- lapply(subject_rows, function(rows) {
    experiment(
        parameters = parameters(
            BW = rows$bw[[1]],
            female = as.numeric(rows$sex[[1]] == "female")
        ),
        dosing = dosing(
            time = 0 [h],
            amount = 100 [mg],
            molec = "drug",
            cmt = "Central"
        ),
        observations = observation_data(
            time = rows$time,
            observable = "C",
            value = rows$concentration
        ),
        start = 0 [h],
        name = rows$id[[1]]
    )
})

studies <- do.call(c, unname(study_list))
studies[1]
```

This conversion is intentionally explicit: it shows which tabular columns have
model semantics. It also exposes a possible future convenience abstraction—a
data-to-experiments helper—without requiring one for the core representation.

More than two categories can be represented by several indicator parameters,
using one category as the reference. Other explicit contrast systems can be
used as well. Character or factor values may be retained in the source data,
but quantities entering numerical model equations should be encoded
numerically.

One possible future abstraction would keep contrast construction at this
data-to-experiments boundary. A reusable specification could declare the full
set and order of levels, the reference level, and the coding scheme, and then
add stable solver-facing parameters while retaining the original categorical
value:

```r
sex_contrast <- categorical_contrast(
    parameter = "sex",
    levels = c("male", "female"),
    reference = "male",
    coding = "treatment"
)

studies <- encode_covariates(studies, sex_contrast)
```

The levels should be declared rather than inferred from the current data so
that fitting subsets and future prediction data use the same parameter schema.
The model equation would continue to refer explicitly to the generated
contrast parameter, such as `sex_female`.

A more extensive alternative would make the categorical effect part of the
model expression itself:

```r
equations(
    CL = CLref *
        (BW / BWref)^theta_BW *
        categorical_effect(
            sex,
            reference = "male",
            female = exp(beta_female)
        )
)
```

Such an abstraction would coordinate model semantics and backend encoding, but
would require categorical covariate metadata to become a persistent part of
the model. Both interfaces above are design suggestions and are not currently
implemented.

## Nonlinear regression

In nonlinear regression, the covariate equation accounts for all systematic
between-individual differences in clearance. Individuals share `CLref`, `V`,
`theta_BW`, and `beta_female`; only their known covariates differ.

The statistical model adds observation error around the model-predicted
concentration.

```{r}
#| label: regression-statistical-model
regression_statistics <- statistical_model(
    C = normal(sd = "sigma")
)
```

### Estimate covariate effects

```{r}
#| label: regression-estimation
regression_specs <- c(
    parameter_specs(
        CLref = 1 [L/h],
        V = 10 [L],
        sigma = 0.1 [mg/L],
        transform = "log"
    ),
    parameter_specs(
        theta_BW = 0.7,
        beta_female = 0,
        transform = "identity"
    )
)

regression_problem <- estimation_problem(
    model = model,
    experiments = studies,
    parameters = regression_specs,
    statistics = regression_statistics
)

regression_fit <- estimate(
    regression_problem,
    engine = optim_engine(
        method = "L-BFGS-B",
        control = list(maxit = 150),
        simulation = deSolve_engine(compiled = TRUE)
    )
)

coef(regression_fit)
```

The positive structural and error-scale quantities use a log transformation.
`theta_BW` and `beta_female` are left on the identity scale because meaningful
estimates can lie on either side of zero.

The fitted covariate relationship can be inspected independently of the ODE.
The calculation below currently recodes the `CL` expression already stored in
`model$equations`. A future abstraction should make model equations reusable
for predictions outside simulation; its design may also require reconsidering
the distinction between equations and observables.

```{r}
#| label: regression-covariate-plot
regression_coef <- coef(regression_fit)

covariate_curve <- expand.grid(
    BW = seq(
        min(covariate_data$bw),
        max(covariate_data$bw),
        length.out = 100
    ),
    female = c(0, 1)
)
covariate_curve$sex <- ifelse(covariate_curve$female == 1, "female", "male")
covariate_curve$CL <- regression_coef$CLref * (covariate_curve$BW / model$parameters$BWref)^regression_coef$theta_BW *
    exp(regression_coef$beta_female * covariate_curve$female)

ggplot(covariate_curve, aes(x = BW, y = CL, colour = sex)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    labs(
        x = "Body weight",
        y = "Typical clearance",
        title = "Estimated clearance covariate relationship"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

## Nonlinear mixed-effects modelling

A covariate model rarely explains all differences between individuals. A
mixed-effects model can retain the same deterministic covariate relationship
while allowing each individual to have a different reference clearance:

\[
CL_{ref,i} = TVCL\exp(\eta_{CL,i}),
\qquad \eta_{CL,i} \sim N(0, \omega_{CL}^2).
\]

Substitution into the earlier equation gives

\[
CL_i = TVCL
       \left(\frac{BW_i}{BW_{ref}}\right)^{\theta_{BW}}
       \exp(\beta_{female} female_i)
       \exp(\eta_{CL,i}).
\]

The random distribution is assigned to the unresolved structural parameter
`CLref`. The final `CL` remains an equation-derived quantity. This keeps the
deterministic covariate model separate from the stochastic population model.

```{r}
#| label: mixed-statistical-model
mixed_statistics <- statistical_model(
    CLref = lognormal(
        median = "TVCL",
        sdlog = "omega_CL"
    ),
    C = normal(sd = "sigma")
)
```

No realized `CLref` values occur in `studies`. During estimation they are
unknown individual random effects, whereas `BW` and `female` remain known
experiment parameters.

### Estimate fixed and random effects

The estimated quantities are the typical clearance, covariate coefficients,
volume, between-individual standard deviation, and residual standard deviation.

```{r}
#| label: mixed-estimation
#| eval: !expr has_nlmixr2
mixed_specs <- c(
    parameter_specs(
        TVCL = 1 [L/h],
        V = 10 [L],
        omega_CL = 0.2,
        sigma = 0.1 [mg/L],
        transform = "log"
    ),
    parameter_specs(
        theta_BW = 0.7,
        beta_female = 0,
        transform = "identity"
    )
)

mixed_problem <- estimation_problem(
    model = model,
    experiments = studies,
    parameters = mixed_specs,
    statistics = mixed_statistics
)

mixed_fit <- estimate(
    mixed_problem,
    engine = nlmixr2_engine(
        control = list(print = 0L, maxOuterIterations = 100L)
    )
)

coef(mixed_fit)
standard_errors(mixed_fit)
```

The mixed-effects result distinguishes population predictions from predictions
conditional on each individual's fitted random effect:

```{r}
#| label: mixed-predictions
#| eval: !expr has_nlmixr2
pred <- fitted(mixed_fit, "PRED")
ipred <- fitted(mixed_fit, "IPRED")

prediction_comparison <- data.frame(
    experiment = ipred$experiment,
    time = ipred$time,
    observed = observations(studies)$value,
    PRED = pred$value,
    IPRED = ipred$value
)

ggplot(prediction_comparison, aes(x = time, group = experiment)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = PRED, linetype = "PRED"), colour = "#3366AA") +
    geom_line(aes(y = IPRED, linetype = "IPRED"), colour = "#3366AA") +
    geom_point(aes(y = observed), colour = "#AA5533", size = 1.2) +
    facet_wrap(~ experiment) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(PRED = "dashed", IPRED = "solid")) +
    labs(x = "Time", y = "Concentration", linetype = NULL) +
    theme_minimal()
```

## Interpretation and current boundaries

The two workflows differ only in the statistical assumption about `CLref`.
The experiment representation and covariate equation are unchanged:

| Concern | Nonlinear regression | Mixed-effects modelling |
|---|---|---|
| Observed covariates | Experiment parameters | Experiment parameters |
| Deterministic covariate effects | Model equations | Model equations |
| Shared coefficients | Parameter specifications | Parameter specifications |
| Unexplained individual variability | None | Individual-level statistical distribution |
| Observation variability | Observation-level statistical distribution | Observation-level statistical distribution |

Continuous covariates may be scalar and constant over an experiment or supplied
as structured interpolation profiles with `interpolate()`. Covariate
measurement error, between-occasion variability, and automatic categorical
contrast construction still require additional behaviour. Keeping observed
covariates as experiment parameters makes the values explicit and allows the
same dynamic model to be used for simulation, nonlinear regression, and
nonlinear mixed-effects estimation.
